title: Two- and three-word verbs: word order
subtitle: look it up / tell them apart / talk me out of it
summary: Decide where the object goes with two- and three-word verbs, and why a pronoun object behaves differently.

lesson.heading: Two- and three-word verbs
lesson.text: When a verb is used with a particular preposition or adverb (a particle), the meaning is often quite different from the meaning of the separate parts. Some of these verbs take an adverb *and* a preposition.

examples.text: I'll quickly **go over** the main points of the report again.
She had to **let** her dress **out** because she'd put on weight.
Do you think he's really likely to **go through with** his threat?
The team has failed to **live up to** earlier expectations.

lesson.note: These verbs are also called phrasal verbs.

lesson.heading: With an object or without?
lesson.text: Many two-word verbs are intransitive - they never take an object. Others work both ways, sometimes with the same meaning and sometimes with a different one.

examples.text: He **grew up** on a farm. / When she **came to** she found herself in hospital.
examples.note: intransitive; also crop up, fall through, get up, move off, shop around, splash out

examples.text: I'll **call back** later. / I'll **call** you **back** when I get home.
examples.note: same meaning either way; also answer back, clear away, cover up, help out, take over, tidy up, wash up

examples.text: The engine **cut out** and the car came to a stop. / I **cut** the picture **out** and kept it.
examples.note: different meanings; also break in, hold out, look out, look up, pick up, split up, turn in, wind up

lesson.heading: Object before or after the adverb
lesson.text: With many transitive two-word verbs the object can go either side of the adverb. We prefer to put a long object after the adverb.

examples.text: I want to **try out** the local food. / I want to **try** the local food **out**.
She had to **clean the kitchen up**.
She had to **clean up the mess in the kitchen**.
examples.note: rather than clean the mess in the kitchen up

lesson.note: Also: bring about, clean up, count out, drink up, gather up, get down, leave out, make up, mess up, shoot down, sort out, throw away, use up.

lesson.text: A pronoun object always sits between the verb and the adverb: You'll have to count me out, not ~~count out me~~.

lesson.heading: Verbs where the object stays in the middle
lesson.text: With some transitive two-word verbs the object always comes between the verb and the adverb, even when it is a noun.

examples.text: I just couldn't **tell the twins apart**.

lesson.note: Also: catch out, hear out, order about, pull to, push to, shut up (= to silence), stand up.

lesson.heading: Verbs where the object follows the preposition
lesson.text: With other transitive two-word verbs the particle is a preposition, so the object always follows it.

examples.text: I **flicked through** a magazine while I was waiting.

lesson.note: Also: account for, act on, approve of, call on, check into, look after, provide for, result from, run into, take against.

lesson.heading: Three-word verbs
lesson.text: With most three-word verbs the object goes after the preposition. A few, however, take the object immediately after the verb, and a second noun phrase goes after the preposition.

examples.text: He really **looks up to** his older brother.
examples.note: also come in for, come up against, cut back on, look down on, put up with

examples.text: She tried to **talk me out of** the plan.
examples.note: also do out of, help on with, let in on, put down as, put up to, take up on

lesson.heading: The five patterns at a glance
rows: Object either side of the adverb
I want to try out the local food. / ... try the local food out.
Pronoun object: always in the middle
You'll have to count me out.
I couldn't tell the twins apart.
She takes after her mother. / He looks up to his older brother.
Three-word verbs with the object first
She tried to talk me out of the plan.

exercises.prompt: I'm not sure how you spell it. I'll ___ in the dictionary.
exercises.explanation: A pronoun object goes between the verb and the adverb, and look up needs an object here.

exercises.statement: I checked into the hotel at about four.
exercises.explanation: Correct. With check into the object follows the preposition.

exercises.prompt: It's freezing in here. Can you ___?
exercises.explanation: With push to the object always stays between the verb and the adverb.

exercises.statement: He was always ordering about everyone, getting them to do his work for him.
exercises.explanation: He was always ordering everyone about. With order about the object comes in the middle.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. The object is a pronoun, so watch where it goes.
exercises.answer: The house is untidy, but I haven't got time to sort it out now.
exercises.explanation: sort out allows either order with a noun, but a pronoun must come before the adverb.

exercises.prompt: Where does the object go with each verb?
categories: In the middle: tell the twins apart
After the particle: take after her mother

exercises.prompt: I know you suspect me of cheating, but you've got to give me a chance to explain myself. At least ___ before making up your mind.
exercises.explanation: hear out keeps its object between the verb and the adverb.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I must get my shoes repaired again. *B:* But they're so old - ... Put B's words in order.
exercises.answer: why don't you just throw them away?
exercises.explanation: throw away takes either order with a noun, but the pronoun them must come before away.

exercises.prompt: There were so many desserts on the menu, I couldn't ___.
exercises.explanation: make up allows the object on either side of the adverb.

exercises.statement: I had always looked Mr Gao up to, so I was shocked to discover what he had done.
exercises.explanation: I had always looked up to Mr Gao. With this three-word verb the object goes after the preposition.

exercises.prompt: When she filled the form in she ___, so they sent it back to her.
exercises.explanation: leave out allows the object on either side of the adverb.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. The object is long, so it belongs at the end.
exercises.answer: The strike by airline pilots messed up the holiday I'd spent months planning.
exercises.explanation: With a long object we prefer to keep the verb and adverb together and put the object last.
